toolUseResult.originalFile:
A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is used to move glass panes, stone slabs, and similar flat panels on site by suction gripping. A suction cup is pressed against the face of the panel, air is removed from the space enclosed between the cup and the panel, and the resulting difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in that enclosed space clamps the cup to the panel so that the panel can be carried.

A suction grip is only as good as its seal. Dust on the panel, a textured or porous surface, a nick in the sealing lip, a change in temperature, or simply the slow permeation and leakage that occurs over minutes of handling will all bleed air back into the enclosed space. As air returns, the clamping force falls. The failure is progressive and, from the point of view of the person holding the panel, silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes until the cup lets go, at which point a heavy panel is already falling.

Vacuum lifting equipment has therefore long been fitted with vacuum monitoring. In one known lifter for transporting loads having an adhesion surface, a suction plate assembly carries projecting annular seals defining a vacuum chamber connected to a main vacuum source, a battery-fed emergency vacuum source that can be started by an emergency switch is additionally provided, and a pressure pickup associated with the vacuum chamber is coupled with a malfunction alarm such that the alarm is turned on when a preset limit pressure is exceeded during vacuum operation [REF:US-5310232-A]. That equipment is a suspended plate assembly with a main vacuum source and a separate emergency vacuum source; the alarm is described as a malfunction alarm tied to a preset limit pressure, and the reference does not describe the limit pressure in terms of the vacuum still needed to keep hold of the load.

Control systems for vacuum lift equipment have also been described in which a programmable controller interprets feedback from vacuum level sensors and battery sensors and responsively provides warnings and limits or alters machine functions, including evaluating a change in measured vacuum level over time to determine a rate of vacuum level change that may be caused by a leak and outputting a warning indication when that rate exceeds a threshold rate [REF:US-10518985-B2]. Such a system is built around a controller with memory, stored records, and machine-function interlocks, and its leak warning is a response to how fast the vacuum is changing rather than to where the vacuum sits relative to the point at which the grip would fail.

Powered suction devices in a hand-carried format are also known. An electric vacuum suction lifter has been described having a main body with a suction surface carrying first and second annular sealing units that bound a sealed space, a control unit, a vacuum pump controlled by the control unit to draw air from the sealed space, a pressure sensing unit that measures the pressure of the sealed space to generate instant pressure information, a battery unit that is charged by external power equipment and powers the control unit, pump, and pressure sensing unit, a start button, a pressure relief button, and at least one handle by which a member gripped by the device can be carried [REF:US-10625955-B2]. In that device the instant pressure information is compared with a high predetermined pressure and a low predetermined pressure: reaching the high predetermined pressure stops the pump, and falling below the low predetermined pressure restarts the pump. A warning unit is described as being operated when the detected battery power is below a predetermined battery power, and warning information relating to pressure is described as being transmitted to an external electronic device. A closely similar electric suction cup has likewise been described, in which the pressure detection unit detects the pressure between the suction cup and the component in real time and the vacuum pump automatically acts again when that pressure is lower than a second predetermined pressure [REF:CN-110630621-B].

Multi-cup handling equipment has been described in which two or more vacuum modules are mounted on a mounting frame, each module having a cup, an electrically powered vacuum pump, a fluid circuit, a controller, and optionally a pressure sensor and a battery, with an interface through which a user selects an operational mode of the modules, and in which each module may include indicators that indicate a functional condition of the module visually or audibly [REF:WO-2022236379-A1].

Two shortcomings persist for a person who is holding a panel in one hand. First, the response to a decaying grip in the known powered devices is to run the pump again: the device treats a falling vacuum as a housekeeping event to be corrected, and the low pressure value at which it acts is chosen with reference to the working vacuum, not with reference to how much grip is left. If the leak is larger than the pump can make up - a torn lip, a dusty or porous panel, a cracked substrate - the pump simply runs while the grip continues to decay, and the user is told nothing until the panel is gone. Second, where a warning is given, it is given either on a condition unrelated to grip (battery state), on a rate of change, or at a preset limit whose relationship to the load-holding capacity of the cup is not established. None of these guarantees the one thing a person carrying a slab actually needs: notice that arrives while the cup is still holding, with grip left over to get the panel down.

There remains a need for a self-contained, cordless, hand-held vacuum lifter that tells the user that the grip is failing at a point on the decay curve at which the grip has not yet failed.

A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is used to move glass panes, stone slabs, and similar flat panels on site by suction gripping. A suction cup is pressed against the face of the panel, air is removed from the space enclosed between the cup and the panel, and the resulting difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in that enclosed space clamps the cup to the panel so that the panel can be carried.

A suction grip is only as good as its seal. Dust on the panel, a textured or porous surface, a nick in the sealing lip, a change in temperature, or simply the slow permeation and leakage that occurs over minutes of handling will all bleed air back into the enclosed space. As air returns, the clamping force falls. The failure is progressive and, from the point of view of the person holding the panel, silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes until the cup lets go, at which point a heavy panel is already falling.

Vacuum lifting equipment has therefore long been fitted with vacuum monitoring. In one known lifter for transporting loads having an adhesion surface, a suction plate assembly carries projecting annular seals defining a vacuum chamber connected to a main vacuum source, a battery-fed emergency vacuum source that can be started by an emergency switch is additionally provided, and a pressure pickup associated with the vacuum chamber is coupled with a malfunction alarm such that the alarm is turned on when a preset limit pressure is exceeded during vacuum operation [REF:US-5310232-A]. That equipment is a suspended plate assembly with a main vacuum source and a separate emergency vacuum source; the alarm is described as a malfunction alarm tied to a preset limit pressure, and the reference does not describe the limit pressure in terms of the vacuum still needed to keep hold of the load.

Control systems for vacuum lift equipment have also been described in which a programmable controller interprets feedback from vacuum level sensors and battery sensors and responsively provides warnings and limits or alters machine functions, including evaluating a change in measured vacuum level over time to determine a rate of vacuum level change that may be caused by a leak and outputting a warning indication when that rate exceeds a threshold rate [REF:US-10518985-B2]. Such a system is built around a controller with memory, stored records, and machine-function interlocks, and its leak warning is a response to how fast the vacuum is changing rather than to where the vacuum sits relative to the point at which the grip would fail.

Powered suction devices in a hand-carried format are also known. An electric vacuum suction lifter has been described having a main body with a suction surface carrying first and second annular sealing units that bound a sealed space, a control unit, a vacuum pump controlled by the control unit to draw air from the sealed space, a pressure sensing unit that measures the pressure of the sealed space to generate instant pressure information, a battery unit that is charged by external power equipment and powers the control unit, pump, and pressure sensing unit, a start button, a pressure relief button, and at least one handle by which a member gripped by the device can be carried [REF:US-10625955-B2]. In that device the instant pressure information is compared with a high predetermined pressure and a low predetermined pressure: reaching the high predetermined pressure stops the pump, and falling below the low predetermined pressure restarts the pump. A warning unit is described as being operated when the detected battery power is below a predetermined battery power, and warning information relating to pressure is described as being transmitted to an external electronic device. This summary introduces a selection of concepts that are described further in the detailed description. It is not intended to identify essential features of the claimed subject matter, nor to limit the scope of the claims.

A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is disclosed. The lifter has a rigid body comprising a handle, and a suction cup carried by the rigid body. The suction cup comprises a flexible sealing lip which, when placed against a workpiece, bounds a sealed region between the suction cup and the workpiece. An electric vacuum pump is disposed within the rigid body and draws air from the sealed region through a port so as to establish a grip vacuum in the sealed region, the grip vacuum holding the suction cup, and hence a load carried by the suction cup, against the workpiece. A pressure sensor monitors the grip vacuum. A warning indicator is carried by the rigid body and is driven by the pressure sensor. A rechargeable battery carried by the rigid body powers the electric vacuum pump.

The grip vacuum is treated throughout this disclosure as a positive magnitude: it is the amount by which the pressure in the sealed region is below the ambient pressure outside the lifter, so that a larger grip vacuum means a firmer grip and a decaying grip is a falling grip vacuum.

The warning indicator activates when the grip vacuum falls to a warning vacuum level. The warning vacuum level is not the level at which the grip fails and is not the level at which the pump is asked to run again. It is a level that is greater than a release vacuum level, the release vacuum level being the grip vacuum below which the suction cup can no longer retain the load. Because the warning vacuum level is above the release vacuum level, the grip vacuum on a decaying grip reaches the warning vacuum level first and the release vacuum level only afterwards. The warning indicator therefore activates while the suction cup is still holding the load, and there is grip in reserve at the moment the user is told. That reserve is what the user spends in getting the panel onto a stand, against a wall, or back onto the stack.

This ordering of levels is what makes the alarm useful in a hand-held tool rather than merely informative. A frame-mounted or suspended lifter can respond to a failing grip by itself, by cutting in a second vacuum source or by refusing to move. A cordless handheld lifter has no such recourse: the only actuator available is the person holding the handle, and a person needs an interval in which to act. Defining the warning threshold with respect to the release vacuum level, rather than with respect to the working vacuum level or with respect to a rate of change, is what makes that interval exist by construction rather than by luck.

In embodiments, the warning indicator remains active for as long as the grip vacuum stays at or below the warning vacuum level, so that a grip which is decaying continuously produces a warning which persists rather than a single transient. In embodiments, the warning indicator is positioned on the rigid body where it is perceptible to a user whose hand is on the handle and whose eyes are on the panel. In embodiments, the pressure sensor is in fluid communication with the sealed region, so that what is monitored is the grip vacuum acting on the workpiece itself rather than a proxy elsewhere in the machine.

Because the electric vacuum pump, the pressure sensor, the warning indicator, and the rechargeable battery are all carried by the rigid body, the lifter grips, monitors, and warns without any hose, cord, or external controller, and can be taken up a ladder or onto a scaffold in one hand.

A method of lifting a workpiece with such a lifter is also disclosed. The method includes placing the flexible sealing lip against the workpiece, drawing air from the sealed region with the electric vacuum pump to establish the grip vacuum, monitoring the grip vacuum with the pressure sensor while the load is carried, and activating the warning indicator when the grip vacuum falls to the warning vacuum level, that is, while the suction cup still retains the load and before the grip vacuum has fallen to the release vacuum level.

horizontal broken lines; the trace is a solid curve. All line work lies well inside the

  means a larger grip vacuum, that is, a firmer grip; the origin is zero grip vacuum.

  order from the top of the drawing area downwards:

  same way.

1	A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is used to move glass panes, stone slabs, and similar flat panels on site by suction gripping. A suction cup is pressed against the face of the panel, air is removed from the space enclosed between the cup and the panel, and the resulting difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in that enclosed space clamps the cup to the panel so that the panel can be carried.
2	
3	A suction grip is only as good as its seal. Dust on the panel, a textured or porous surface, a nick in the sealing lip, a change in temperature, or simply the slow permeation and leakage that occurs over minutes of handling will all bleed air back into the enclosed space. As air returns, the clamping force falls. The failure is progressive and, from the point of view of the person holding the panel, silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes until the cup lets go, at which point a heavy panel is already falling.
4	
5	Vacuum lifting equipment has therefore long been fitted with vacuum monitoring. In one known lifter for transporting loads having an adhesion surface, a suction plate assembly carries projecting annular seals defining a vacuum chamber connected to a main vacuum source, a battery-fed emergency vacuum source that can be started by an emergency switch is additionally provided, and a pressure pickup associated with the vacuum chamber is coupled with a malfunction alarm such that the alarm is turned on when a preset limit pressure is exceeded during vacuum operation [REF:US-5310232-A]. That equipment is a suspended plate assembly with a main vacuum source and a separate emergency vacuum source; the alarm is described as a malfunction alarm tied to a preset limit pressure, and the reference does not describe the limit pressure in terms of the vacuum still needed to keep hold of the load.
6	
7	Control systems for vacuum lift equipment have also been described in which a programmable controller interprets feedback from vacuum level sensors and battery sensors and responsively provides warnings and limits or alters machine functions, including evaluating a change in measured vacuum level over time to determine a rate of vacuum level change that may be caused by a leak and outputting a warning indication when that rate exceeds a threshold rate [REF:US-10518985-B2]. Such a system is built around a controller with memory, stored records, and machine-function interlocks, and its leak warning is a response to how fast the vacuum is changing rather than to where the vacuum sits relative to the point at which the grip would fail.
8	
9	Powered suction devices in a hand-carried format are also known. An electric vacuum suction lifter has been described having a main body with a suction surface carrying first and second annular sealing units that bound a sealed space, a control unit, a vacuum pump controlled by the control unit to draw air from the sealed space, a pressure sensing unit that measures the pressure of the sealed space to generate instant pressure information, a battery unit that is charged by external power equipment and powers the control unit, pump, and pressure sensing unit, a start button, a pressure relief button, and at least one handle by which a member gripped by the device can be carried [REF:US-10625955-B2]. In that device the instant pressure information is compared with a high predetermined pressure and a low predetermined pressure: reaching the high predetermined pressure stops the pump, and falling below the low predetermined pressure restarts the pump. A warning unit is described as being operated when the detected battery power is below a predetermined battery power, and warning information relating to pressure is described as being transmitted to an external electronic device. A closely similar electric suction cup has likewise been described, in which the pressure detection unit detects the pressure between the suction cup and the component in real time and the vacuum pump automatically acts again when that pressure is lower than a second predetermined pressure [REF:CN-110630621-B].
10	
11	Other hand-carried suction devices give the user a reading or a signal of some kind. A digital display suction cup has been described comprising a suction cup and a handle structure, the handle structure carrying a battery and a vacuum electric pump connected to the suction cup through an air pipe, together with an air pressure sensor, a display screen, a switch button, a pressure relief valve, and a USB charging port, the display screen displaying the negative pressure value of the suction cup and the battery power [REF:US-2024424646-A1]. What that device offers the operator is a number to be read: negative pressure is monitored and displayed in real time, and the reference does not describe a level at which the device itself declares that the grip is going. A portable electric carrying suction cup structure has likewise been described in which a vacuum pump is arranged on a suction cup body having a handle fixed at its upper end, a control unit is connected between the power supply part and the vacuum pump, and the control unit is provided with a pressure gauge, with a light source that displays different usage states, and with a buzzer that sends out alarm sounds according to different usage states, air being pumped out continuously so as to avoid loosening and falling during movement [REF:CN-2806399-Y]. There again the answer to a decaying grip is to keep pumping, and the alarm follows a usage state rather than any stated relationship to the vacuum at which the cup would let the load go.
12	
13	A portable hand grab has also been described including one or more suction cups, at least one handle, at least one electrical vacuum pump, at least one vacuum sensor for detecting a vacuum level in the suction volume between a cup and an attachment surface, and an electronic controller configured to control the pump to evacuate the suction volume when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being less than a preselected minimum vacuum level, optionally with a power storage unit and with an attach indicator that the controller activates when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being greater than a preselected safe vacuum level [REF:WO-2017156581-A1]. The indicator described there reports that attachment has been achieved, that is, it responds to a vacuum level lying above a threshold; the threshold that governs a falling vacuum in that device is the minimum vacuum level at which the pump is run again.
14	
15	Cordless hand tools that grip by suction are themselves long established. A cordless wand device for grasping objects such as silicon wafers has been described having a housing with a hollow interior, a tip whose perimeter region is contoured to form an airtight seal against the object, a power source and a vacuum pump positioned within the housing, and light emitting diodes of different colours that indicate to an operator whether the power source is sufficiently charged to generate sufficient suction force to safely grasp the object, sufficiency being determined from the voltage drop across resistors connected to the power source [REF:US-5374090-A]. That indication is drawn from the state of the power source rather than from a measurement of the vacuum that is holding the object. In a sucker for plate glass, a sucker body carries a manually operated vacuum pump, a sensor communicating with the suction channel by way of a piston lever that moves in proportion to the degree of vacuum, and a sound generator that is turned on through a switch closed by the piston lever when the degree of vacuum sensed reaches a predetermined value [REF:US-5184858-A]. The vacuum in that device is raised by hand, and the predetermined value at which the sound generator is turned on is the working stroke of a limit switch; the reference does not relate that value to the vacuum below which the sucker would cease to retain the sheet it is carrying.
16	
17	Multi-cup handling equipment has been described in which two or more vacuum modules are mounted on a mounting frame, each module having a cup, an electrically powered vacuum pump, a fluid circuit, a controller, and optionally a pressure sensor and a battery, with an interface through which a user selects an operational mode of the modules, and in which each module may include indicators that indicate a functional condition of the module visually or audibly [REF:WO-2022236379-A1].
18	
19	Two shortcomings persist for a person who is holding a panel in one hand. First, the response to a decaying grip in the known powered devices is to run the pump again: the device treats a falling vacuum as a housekeeping event to be corrected, and the low pressure value at which it acts is chosen with reference to the working vacuum, not with reference to how much grip is left. If the leak is larger than the pump can make up - a torn lip, a dusty or porous panel, a cracked substrate - the pump simply runs while the grip continues to decay, and the user is told nothing until the panel is gone. Second, where a signal is given, it is given on a condition unrelated to grip such as battery state, on the achievement of attachment, on a rate of change, as a displayed number that the operator must read and interpret while carrying a slab, or at a preset limit whose relationship to the load-holding capacity of the cup is not established. None of these guarantees the one thing a person carrying a slab actually needs: notice that arrives while the cup is still holding, with grip left over to get the panel down.
20	
21	Third, much of the equipment that does monitor vacuum carefully is not something a person can carry. It sits on a frame, a boom, or a mounting frame, and it depends on a hose to a remote vacuum source, a mains or vehicle supply, a reservoir, or a controller and interface that are not part of the tool. On such equipment the decision about a failing grip can be taken away from the operator and acted on by the machine. A tool that is to be taken up a ladder or onto a scaffold in one hand has no tether and no machine to act for it, so the sensing, the decision, and the warning must all be carried on the tool itself and be powered from it.
22	
23	There remains a need for a self-contained, cordless, hand-held vacuum lifter that carries its own pump, sensing, warning, and power, and that tells the user that the grip is failing at a point on the decay curve at which the grip has not yet failed.
24

In a sucker for plate glass, a sucker body carries a manually operated vacuum pump, a sensor communicating with the suction channel by way of a piston lever that moves in proportion to the degree of vacuum, and a sound generator that is turned on through a switch closed by the piston lever when the degree of vacuum sensed reaches a predetermined value [REF:US-5184858-A]. The vacuum in that device is raised by hand, and the predetermined value at which the sound generator is turned on is the working stroke of a limit switch; the reference does not relate that value to the vacuum below which the sucker would cease to retain the sheet it is carrying.

Multi-cup handling equipment has been described in which two or more vacuum modules are mounted on a mounting frame, each module having a cup, an electrically powered vacuum pump, a fluid circuit, a controller, and optionally a pressure sensor and a battery, with an interface through which a user selects an operational mode of the modules, and in which each module may include indicators that indicate a functional condition of the module visually or audibly [REF:WO-2022236379-A1].

Two shortcomings persist for a person who is holding a panel in one hand. First, the response to a decaying grip in the known powered devices is to run the pump again: the device treats a falling vacuum as a housekeeping event to be corrected, and the low pressure value at which it acts is chosen with reference to the working vacuum, not with reference to how much grip is left. If the leak is larger than the pump can make up - a torn lip, a dusty or porous panel, a cracked substrate - the pump simply runs while the grip continues to decay, and the user is told nothing until the panel is gone. Second, where a signal is given, it is given on a condition unrelated to grip such as battery state, on the achievement of attachment, on a rate of change, as a displayed number that the operator must read and interpret while carrying a slab, or at a preset limit whose relationship to the load-holding capacity of the cup is not established. None of these guarantees the one thing a person carrying a slab actually needs: notice that arrives while the cup is still holding, with grip left over to get the panel down.

Third, much of the equipment that does monitor vacuum carefully is not something a person can carry. It sits on a frame, a boom, or a mounting frame, and it depends on a hose to a remote vacuum source, a mains or vehicle supply, a reservoir, or a controller and interface that are not part of the tool. On such equipment the decision about a failing grip can be taken away from the operator and acted on by the machine. A tool that is to be taken up a ladder or onto a scaffold in one hand has no tether and no machine to act for it, so the sensing, the decision, and the warning must all be carried on the tool itself and be powered from it.

There remains a need for a self-contained, cordless, hand-held vacuum lifter that carries its own pump, sensing, warning, and power, and that tells the user that the grip is failing at a point on the decay curve at which the grip has not yet failed.

21	The operation of the warning function is described with reference to FIG. 4, which plots grip vacuum on a vacuum axis 70 against time on a time axis 72. A grip vacuum trace 60 shows the history of a grip that begins sound and then decays.
22	
23	The electric vacuum pump 20 first raises the grip vacuum to a working vacuum level 62, which is the grip vacuum at which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is fit to lift. The user then lifts and carries the workpiece 50. If the seal between the flexible sealing lip 12 and the workpiece 50 is imperfect, because of dust or grit under the lip, a textured or porous face, a damaged lip, or flexing of the workpiece 50, air bleeds into the sealed region 18 and the grip vacuum trace 60 falls away from the working vacuum level 62.
24	
25	Two levels lie below the working vacuum level 62 on the vacuum axis 70. The lower of the two is the release vacuum level 66, at which the suction cup 10 lets go. The higher of the two is the warning vacuum level 64, at which the warning indicator 32 activates. Because the warning vacuum level 64 is greater than the release vacuum level 66, a falling grip vacuum trace 60 crosses the warning vacuum level 64 before it reaches the release vacuum level 66. The warning indicator 32 therefore activates at a moment when the grip vacuum is still above the release vacuum level 66 and the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load. The warning indicator 32 is thus configured to activate before the load can be dropped. The elapsed time between the crossing of the warning vacuum level 64 and the arrival of the grip vacuum trace 60 at the release vacuum level 66 is the warning interval 68. The warning interval 68 begins when the grip vacuum falls to the warning vacuum level 64 and ends when the grip vacuum falls to the release vacuum level 66.
26	
27	The warning interval 68 is the technical product of the ordering of the two levels, and it is the point of the arrangement. During the warning interval 68 the user still has a held load and a working grip, and can walk the workpiece 50 to a stand, set it against a wall, or lower it onto the stack. Setting the workpiece 50 down during the warning interval 68 ends the lift without a drop. Nothing in the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 needs to intervene, and nothing needs to be fast: the reserve of grip between the warning vacuum level 64 and the release vacuum level 66 is what buys the time, and it exists by construction because of where the warning vacuum level 64 has been set.
28	
29	This is a different design decision from choosing a low pressure value at which to run a pump again. A restart threshold is chosen with reference to the working vacuum level 62: it is placed just below the working vacuum level 62 so that the grip is topped up frequently and the pump cycles little. Such a threshold says nothing about how much grip remains, and a device that responds to crossing it by running its pump will, when the leak exceeds the pump's capacity, run the pump all the way down through the release vacuum level 66 without ever telling the user that the grip is going. The warning vacuum level 64 is instead chosen with reference to the release vacuum level 66, from below the working vacuum level 62 and above the point of failure, precisely so that its crossing carries the meaning that the grip is failing and the panel is still held. It is also a different decision from warning on a rate of change: a rate-of-change warning fires on a fast leak regardless of how much grip is left, and stays silent on a slow leak that has nonetheless eaten all the reserve.
30	
31	The distinction matters more for a hand-carried tool than for equipment on a frame or a boom. Frame-mounted and suspended lifters can be given their own remedies for a failing grip, such as a second vacuum source, a reservoir, or an interlock that refuses further motion. A cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has none of these: the only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle 16, and a person needs to be told while there is still something to be done. Defining the warning vacuum level 64 with respect to the release vacuum level 66 is what puts the warning inside the window in which the user can act.
32	
33	Carrying the electric vacuum pump 20, the pressure sensor 30, the warning indicator 32, and the rechargeable battery 40 on the rigid body 14 is what makes that window available at all, and it solves a problem that a tethered arrangement cannot. A lifter that took its vacuum through a hose, its power through a cord, or its decision from a controller external to the rigid body 14 would put part of the chain that has to react to a failing seal somewhere other than in the user's hand. Length of hose between a remote vacuum source and the suction cup 10 adds evacuated volume, and, for the reason given above, added evacuated volume buffers a leak and slows the fall in grip vacuum that the pressure sensor 30 has to see. A decision taken off the tool has to be carried back to the user over the same tether, and the tether is itself what stops the tool from going up a ladder or onto a scaffold. Because the sealed region 18 is evacuated by the electric vacuum pump 20 within the rigid body 14, is watched by the pressure sensor 30 carried by the rigid body 14, and is reported by the warning indicator 32 carried by the rigid body 14, all of them powered by the rechargeable battery 40 carried by the rigid body 14, the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 establishes the grip vacuum, monitors the grip vacuum, and activates the warning indicator 32 without connection to any hose, cord, or controller external to the rigid body 14. The whole chain, from the seal that is failing to the person who must act on it, is in the one hand that is holding the load.
34	
35	In embodiments, the warning indicator 32 remains active for as long as the grip vacuum remains at or below the warning vacuum level 64, and deactivates when the grip vacuum returns above the warning vacuum level 64. A decaying grip therefore produces a warning that persists and grows more urgent in context rather than a single transient that a user in a noisy environment may miss.
36	
37	In embodiments, activation of the warning indicator 32 when the grip vacuum falls to the warning vacuum level 64 does not depend on whether the electric vacuum pump 20 is running. When a leak is larger than the electric vacuum pump 20 can make up, the grip vacuum falls to the warning vacuum level 64 while the electric vacuum pump 20 is still running, and the warning indicator 32 activates then and there rather than waiting for the electric vacuum pump 20 to give up. The user is thus told about the grip, which is the thing that is failing, and is not left to infer it from the behaviour of the pump, which is not.
38	
39	In embodiments, the warning vacuum level 64 is set so that the reserve of grip between the warning vacuum level 64 and the release vacuum level 66 corresponds to the whole of the load-holding margin that the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is designed to keep for the workpiece 50 it is rated to carry: the crossing of the warning vacuum level 64 then marks the point at which the grip has ceased to be sound, not the point at which it has nearly gone.

The warning indicator 32 therefore activates at a moment when the grip vacuum is still above the release vacuum level 66 and the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load. The warning indicator 32 is thus configured to activate before the load can be dropped. The elapsed time between the crossing of the warning vacuum level 64 and the arrival of the grip vacuum trace 60 at the release vacuum level 66 is the warning interval 68. The warning interval 68 begins when the grip vacuum falls to the warning vacuum level 64 and ends when the grip vacuum falls to the release vacuum level 66.

The warning interval 68 is the technical product of the ordering of the two levels, and it is the point of the arrangement. During the warning interval 68 the user still has a held load and a working grip, and can walk the workpiece 50 to a stand, set it against a wall, or lower it onto the stack. Setting the workpiece 50 down during the warning interval 68 ends the lift without a drop. Nothing in the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 needs to intervene, and nothing needs to be fast: the reserve of grip between the warning vacuum level 64 and the release vacuum level 66 is what buys the time, and it exists by construction because of where the warning vacuum level 64 has been set.

This is a different design decision from choosing a low pressure value at which to run a pump again. A restart threshold is chosen with reference to the working vacuum level 62: it is placed just below the working vacuum level 62 so that the grip is topped up frequently and the pump cycles little. Such a threshold says nothing about how much grip remains, and a device that responds to crossing it by running its pump will, when the leak exceeds the pump's capacity, run the pump all the way down through the release vacuum level 66 without ever telling the user that the grip is going. The warning vacuum level 64 is instead chosen with reference to the release vacuum level 66, from below the working vacuum level 62 and above the point of failure, precisely so that its crossing carries the meaning that the grip is failing and the panel is still held. It is also a different decision from warning on a rate of change: a rate-of-change warning fires on a fast leak regardless of how much grip is left, and stays silent on a slow leak that has nonetheless eaten all the reserve.

The distinction matters more for a hand-carried tool than for equipment on a frame or a boom. Frame-mounted and suspended lifters can be given their own remedies for a failing grip, such as a second vacuum source, a reservoir, or an interlock that refuses further motion. A cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has none of these: the only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle 16, and a person needs to be told while there is still something to be done. Defining the warning vacuum level 64 with respect to the release vacuum level 66 is what puts the warning inside the window in which the user can act.

Carrying the electric vacuum pump 20, the pressure sensor 30, the warning indicator 32, and the rechargeable battery 40 on the rigid body 14 is what makes that window available at all, and it solves a problem that a tethered arrangement cannot. A lifter that took its vacuum through a hose, its power through a cord, or its decision from a controller external to the rigid body 14 would put part of the chain that has to react to a failing seal somewhere other than in the user's hand. Length of hose between a remote vacuum source and the suction cup 10 adds evacuated volume, and, for the reason given above, added evacuated volume buffers a leak and slows the fall in grip vacuum that the pressure sensor 30 has to see. A decision taken off the tool has to be carried back to the user over the same tether, and the tether is itself what stops the tool from going up a ladder or onto a scaffold. Because the sealed region 18 is evacuated by the electric vacuum pump 20 within the rigid body 14, is watched by the pressure sensor 30 carried by the rigid body 14, and is reported by the warning indicator 32 carried by the rigid body 14, all of them powered by the rechargeable battery 40 carried by the rigid body 14, the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 establishes the grip vacuum, monitors the grip vacuum, and activates the warning indicator 32 without connection to any hose, cord, or controller external to the rigid body 14. The whole chain, from the seal that is failing to the person who must act on it, is in the one hand that is holding the load.

In embodiments, the warning indicator 32 remains active for as long as the grip vacuum remains at or below the warning vacuum level 64, and deactivates when the grip vacuum returns above the warning vacuum level 64. A decaying grip therefore produces a warning that persists and grows more urgent in context rather than a single transient that a user in a noisy environment may miss.

In embodiments, activation of the warning indicator 32 when the grip vacuum falls to the warning vacuum level 64 does not depend on whether the electric vacuum pump 20 is running. When a leak is larger than the electric vacuum pump 20 can make up, the grip vacuum falls to the warning vacuum level 64 while the electric vacuum pump 20 is still running, and the warning indicator 32 activates then and there rather than waiting for the electric vacuum pump 20 to give up. The user is thus told about the grip, which is the thing that is failing, and is not left to infer it from the behaviour of the pump, which is not.

In embodiments, the warning vacuum level 64 is set so that the reserve of grip between the warning vacuum level 64 and the release vacuum level 66 corresponds to the whole of the load-holding margin that the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is designed to keep for the workpiece 50 it is rated to carry: the crossing of the warning vacuum level 64 then marks the point at which the grip has ceased to be sound, not the point at which it has nearly gone.

input.content: A cordless handheld vacuum lifter has a rigid body with a handle and a suction cup whose flexible sealing lip bounds a sealed region against a workpiece such as a glass or stone panel. An electric vacuum pump within the rigid body draws air from the sealed region through a port to establish a grip vacuum that retains a load. A pressure sensor monitors the grip vacuum, a rechargeable battery powers the pump, and a warning indicator driven by the pressure sensor activates when the grip vacuum falls to a warning vacuum level greater than the release vacuum level at which the suction cup would let go, warning the user while the cup still holds the load. The pump, sensor, indicator and battery are all carried by the rigid body, so the lifter grips, monitors and warns without connection to any hose, cord or external controller.

input.summary: Read all ten references, then amended both independent claims to recite the self-contained, everything-on-the-body architecture in addition to the release-referenced warning threshold, added the specification passage that explains the technical problem that architecture solves, and addressed the five previously uncited references in the Background. Separately fixed every mechanical defect the reviewer listed: all nine drafting notes are gone, the cross-reference section now reads "Not applicable.", claim wording was brought into the description's own vocabulary, the two oversized figure briefs were rewritten under the limit, and the drawing plan was redistributed so no sheet carries more than eight numerals while all thirty-two numerals still appear on a sheet.
reasoning: Claim 1 already carried the feature the search found nowhere in the art (the warning vacuum level defined as greater than the release vacuum level, not as a fraction of the working vacuum). I kept that as the primary ground and added the second unmatched feature rather than replacing it: the pump, pressure sensor, warning indicator and rechargeable battery are all carried by the rigid body, so the lifter establishes, monitors and warns without connection to any hose, cord or controller external to the rigid body.

That second clause costs almost no scope. Claim 1's preamble already said cordless handheld, the pump was already 'disposed within the rigid body', and the battery and indicator were already 'carried by the rigid body'. Only the pressure sensor had to be pinned to the body. What the clause buys is a positive recitation of the architecture rather than an implication drawn from the word 'cordless'.

Which feature clears which reference. The release-referenced threshold clears US-10625955-B2 and CN-110630621-B, whose low predetermined pressure is a pump-restart point measured against the high predetermined pressure, and whose warning unit fires on battery power; it clears WO-2017156581-A1, whose indicator activates when vacuum is GREATER than a safe level (an attach-achieved signal) and whose falling-vacuum threshold is the minimum level at which the pump runs again; it clears US-10518985-B2, whose leak warning is a rate-of-change threshold; and it clears US-5310232-A and US-5184858-A, whose alarms are tied to a preset limit or a switch trip point with no stated relation to the vacuum still needed to hold the load.

The self-containment clause is what carries claim 1 clear of the two references that come closest on hardware. US-2024424646-A1 puts battery, pump, sensor and display in a handle structure but connects the pump to the cup through an air pipe and gives the operator a displayed number rather than a device-generated warning level; WO-2022236379-A1 and US-10518985-B2 are frame, boom and machine equipment with an external interface, master controller, harness or reservoir. CN-2806399-Y has a buzzer, but it sounds according to usage state and its answer to leakage is continuous pumping.

I deliberately did not add: any indicator modality, any numeric threshold, any sensor type, any battery particulars, any design rule for setting the warning level. The disclosure says none of those, and the previous draft's nine drafting notes were the honest record of that. Those notes could not stay in a filing package, so I removed them and left the description functional where the source is silent. Nothing was invented to fill the holes.

Claim 9 recited indicator modality (visual, audible, vibratory emitters). The disclosure never states a modality, so the claim had no support and its own note said so. I replaced it with the inventor's own second claim, that the warning indicator activates before the load can be dropped, and added that sentence to the description in the same words.

New claim 10 replaces the old one, which had become redundant once self-containment moved into claim 1. It now recites that the evacuated volume consists of the sealed region, the port and the suction passage, so a leak of a given size produces a rapid and therefore detectable fall. That is a fallback with independent value against US-5310232-A and US-10518985-B2, both of which use a vacuum vessel or reservoir that would buffer exactly that fall.

Description support was widened for the new claim 1 clause with a paragraph stating the problem the architecture solves: a remote source reached through a hose adds evacuated volume that buffers a leak and slows the fall the sensor has to see; a decision taken off the tool has to be carried back over the same tether; and the tether is what keeps the tool off a ladder. That paragraph, and the parallel Background paragraph, are the material a later argument would be built from.

The reviewer's two warnings were partly false positives but not worth defending. 'the panel' in claim 20 did have an antecedent in the same claim, and 'the modality' sat inside a drafting note rather than in claim language. Both disappeared with the rewrite. The ten unsupported claim words were real 112(a) exposure and were fixed by using the description's own words (below rather than less, does not depend on whether the pump is running rather than irrespective, during a warning interval that begins and ends rather than after) and by adding the words unconnected, dropped and consists to the description where the claims need them.

The drawing plan was redistributed rather than trimmed. FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 each listed nineteen numerals; the pneumatic structure now sits on FIG. 2 (eight numerals) and the entire sensing, warning and power chain on FIG. 3 (eight numerals), with the exhaust outlet moved to FIG. 1 to keep every sheet at or below eight. Every part removed from a sheet is described there generically as an unnumbered block, duct or arch, and no numeral definition or supporting text was deleted to satisfy the check. FIG. 1 now carries a proper broken cutting-plane line 2-2 with both endpoints and both viewing arrows specified, and FIG. 2 is taken on that line.

input.prior_art_strategy: Every reference in the index is now addressed in the Background by what its file actually teaches. The art divides into three groups and the claims are drawn to fall outside all three. The powered hand-carried cups (US-10625955-B2, CN-110630621-B, US-2024424646-A1, CN-2806399-Y, WO-2017156581-A1) all treat a falling vacuum as a pump-control or display event: their low threshold is measured from the working vacuum and its crossing starts the pump, shows a number, or reports a usage state. The heavy equipment (US-5310232-A, US-10518985-B2, WO-2022236379-A1) monitors vacuum well but does so from a frame or boom, with a reservoir, a harness, an emergency source, or an external controller and interface, and its warnings key on a preset limit, a rate of change, or battery condition. The early cordless and manual tools (US-5374090-A, US-5184858-A) indicate from power-source voltage or from a limit switch closed by a piston lever. Claim 1 therefore recites two things together that no reference has: a warning vacuum level defined as greater than the release vacuum level at which the cup ceases to retain the load, so the warning necessarily precedes release, and a lifter in which the pump, sensor, indicator and battery are all on the rigid body so the whole chain from failing seal to acting person is in the hand holding the load. Claim 4 is the sharpest single fallback, since it forecloses the restart-threshold devices by requiring the warning to fire while the pump is still running; claim 10 forecloses the reservoir-buffered systems; claim 2 forecloses transient-only indicators.

data.prior_art_strategy: Every reference in the index is now addressed in the Background by what its file actually teaches. The art divides into three groups and the claims are drawn to fall outside all three. The powered hand-carried cups (US-10625955-B2, CN-110630621-B, US-2024424646-A1, CN-2806399-Y, WO-2017156581-A1) all treat a falling vacuum as a pump-control or display event: their low threshold is measured from the working vacuum and its crossing starts the pump, shows a number, or reports a usage state. The heavy equipment (US-5310232-A, US-10518985-B2, WO-2022236379-A1) monitors vacuum well but does so from a frame or boom, with a reservoir, a harness, an emergency source, or an external controller and interface, and its warnings key on a preset limit, a rate of change, or battery condition. The early cordless and manual tools (US-5374090-A, US-5184858-A) indicate from power-source voltage or from a limit switch closed by a piston lever. Claim 1 therefore recites two things together that no reference has: a warning vacuum level defined as greater than the release vacuum level at which the cup ceases to retain the load, so the warning necessarily precedes release, and a lifter in which the pump, sensor, indicator and battery are all on the rigid body so the whole chain from failing seal to acting person is in the hand holding the load. Claim 4 is the sharpest single fallback, since it forecloses the restart-threshold devices by requiring the warning to fire while the pump is still running; claim 10 forecloses the reservoir-buffered systems; claim 2 forecloses transient-only indicators.
data.answer: Both independent claims now recite, in their own terms, the two features the search found in no reference. Claim 1 keeps the warning vacuum level defined as greater than the release vacuum level at which the suction cup ceases to retain the load, and adds that the electric vacuum pump, pressure sensor, warning indicator and rechargeable battery are all carried by the rigid body such that the lifter establishes the grip vacuum, monitors it and activates the warning indicator without connection to any hose, cord or controller external to the rigid body. Method claim 15 carries the same pair. The second feature cost almost no scope, because the preamble, the pump and the battery were already tied to the body; only the sensor had to be pinned down. The detailed description now supports that clause in the same words and explains the problem it solves: hose length adds evacuated volume that buffers a leak and slows the fall the sensor must detect, a decision taken off the tool has to travel back to the user over the same tether, and the tether is what keeps the tool off a ladder. The Background addresses all ten references, including the five that were previously uncited. Separately, every mechanical defect in the review is fixed: the nine drafting notes are gone, the cross-reference section reads "Not applicable.", the unsupported indicator-modality claim was replaced by the disclosure's own "activates before the load can be dropped", claim vocabulary was aligned with the description, both oversized figure briefs are now well under 2800 characters, and the drawing plan was redistributed so that all thirty-two numerals appear on a sheet with no sheet carrying more than eight.
